name: Cloudflare Workers
summary: Functions that run in V8 isolates on Cloudflare’s network, close to the user, with almost no cold start.
intro: Workers don’t use containers or VMs per function. Each Cloudflare machine runs the V8 JavaScript engine (the one in Chrome and Node.js) once, and every Worker runs inside it as an isolate: a sandboxed context with its own memory. One process can hold hundreds or thousands of isolates and switch between them. Cloudflare says an isolate starts about a hundred times faster than a Node process in a container or VM and uses an order of magnitude less memory, so there’s no real cold start to design around.

Your code runs in Cloudflare data centres around the world, in whichever one is nearest the user. JavaScript, TypeScript, Python and Rust are supported directly, and other languages can compile to WebAssembly. Workers talk to Cloudflare’s storage (R2, KV, D1, Durable Objects) through bindings rather than network credentials. The paid plan starts at $5 a month with 10 million requests and 30 million CPU milliseconds included; you’re billed for CPU time, not time spent waiting on the network.
strengths: Starts in a fraction of a container’s time, so scale-from-zero is effectively free
Runs near every user by default, with no regions to pick
Billing counts CPU time only, so a Worker that waits on slow APIs stays cheap
The runtime, `workerd`, is open source, so you can run the same code locally or self-host it
limits: Not a full Node.js or Linux environment: no arbitrary binaries, and some npm packages won’t run
128 MB of memory per isolate, and CPU time is capped (10 ms on the Free plan, up to 5 minutes on Paid)
A Worker’s code is capped at 64 MiB uncompressed, which rules out large dependencies or bundled models
Running near users helps little if your database is in one region far away

story: In 2017 Cloudflare was, at its core, an HTTP cache running in 117 locations, and customers kept asking for behaviour its settings didn’t cover: their own cache rules, custom load balancing, bespoke security checks. Each answer meant building another product feature. As the launch post put it, “We can keep adding features forever, but we’ll never cover every possible use case this way.” The alternative was to let customers run their own code on Cloudflare’s servers.

Kenton Varda, who wrote most of Google’s open-source Protocol Buffers v2 and co-founded Sandstorm.io, led the work and announced Workers on September 29, 2017. Giving every customer a VM or container in every location was out of the question: VMs needed hundreds of megabytes of RAM and typically took tens of seconds to boot. So Workers ran JavaScript in V8 isolates, many to a process. It became available to everyone on March 13, 2018, at $0.50 per million requests with a $5 monthly minimum.

Workers grew from small scripts that rewrite requests into a full platform: Durable Objects added consistent state in 2020, the `workerd` runtime was open-sourced in 2022, and Containers arrived in beta in 2025 for code that doesn’t fit in an isolate.

choices.choice: V8 isolates instead of containers or VMs
choices.why: Code has to run in every data centre, on demand, for every customer. Isolates share one runtime process, start in milliseconds and use a few megabytes, so Cloudflare can afford to keep almost anyone’s code ready almost everywhere.
Varda called V8 “arguably the most scrutinized code sandbox in the history of computing”, backed by Chrome’s security team, and web developers already knew the language.
Instead of inventing request hooks, Workers adopted an existing web standard. Its asynchronous model lets one script make several subrequests in series or in parallel and combine the results.

timeline.text: Kenton Varda announces Workers on September 29
Generally available on March 13; isolates explained in “Cloud Computing without Containers”
Durable Objects bring strongly consistent state to the edge
The `workerd` runtime is open-sourced under Apache 2.0
Workers AI runs models on GPUs in Cloudflare’s network
Cloudflare Containers enter public beta in June, alongside Workers
